translation: Two other small pictures with scalloped edges, presumably from the same year, show the same child, but slighter, in a dress with frills and balloon sleeves.
In the first, she playfully snuggled up against a woman with a massive body, clad in one piece in a dress with wide stripes, her hair pulled up into large rolls.
On the other, she raises her left fist, her right is held by the hand of a tall man in a light jacket and pleated trousers, with a nonchalant posture.
The two photos were taken on the same day in front of a small wall topped with a border of flowers, in a paved courtyard.
Above the heads, there is a clothesline with a pin still clinging to it.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but the paper of the booklet is more ordinary and the gold trim has disappeared—presumably intended for the same family distribution, shows a little girl of about four years old, serious, almost sad despite a chubby good-natured face under short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back by clips to which ribbons are attached like butterflies.
The left hand rests on the same fully visible, Louis XVI style carved table.
She appears squeezed into her bodice, her suspender skirt pulled up in the front due to a prominent belly, possibly a sign of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment, and they looked handsome in their soldier uniforms.
On the evening of the conscription review, they went around the cafes to celebrate the honor of being recognized as real men.
Before the regiment, they were still just kids and weren't worth anything on the job market or in marriage.
Afterwards, they could have a wife and children.
The uniform they paraded around the neighborhood during their leaves, enveloped them in patriotic beauty and virtual sacrifice.
The shadow of the victorious fighters, the GIs, hovered around them.
The coarse cloth of the jacket, brushed against when one stood on tiptoe to kiss them, embodied the absolute division between the world of men and that of women.
Seeing them stirred feelings of heroism.

Beneath the unchanging, the posters from last year's circus with Roger Lanzac's photo, the first communion pictures distributed to mates, The Chansonniers Club on Radio Luxembourg, the days were filled with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, people would crowd around the window of the general electric store to watch television.
Cafes were investing in buying a station to attract customers.
On the sides of the hills wound motocross tracks, and one could watch the deafening machines go up and down all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce with its new buzzwords, "initiative", "dynamism", shook the routine of cities.
Between the carnival and the fair, the Commercial Fortnight was setting up as a spring ritual.
In the downtown streets, loudspeakers blared encouragements to buy, interspersed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine, to win the Simca or the dining room set.

On the podium, at the town hall square, a local host was getting laughs with jokes from Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard, rallying candidates for Amateur Night or Double or Nothing, just like on the radio.
Seated in a corner of the podium, the Queen of Commerce sat on her throne with her crown.
The merchandise moved forward in festive colors.
People would say "things change" or "you shouldn't stagnate, it's dulling to stay at home".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They didn't have enough talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but hadn't seen.
So, neither Jewish children being loaded onto trains for Auschwitz, nor the starved dead collected in the morning in the Warsaw ghetto, nor the 10,000 degrees in Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history classes, documentaries, and films would later not dispel: neither the crematory ovens nor the atomic bomb were in the same era as black market butter, alarms, and trips to the basement.
They segued by comparison to the previous war, The Great one, that of '14, won in blood and glory a man's war that the women of the table listened to with respect.
They were talking about the Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about the gassed victims, about the bells of November 11, 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child who had gone to the front had returned.
They contrasted the soldiers in the trench mud with the prisoners of '40, warm and sheltered for five years, who hadn't even had bombs dropped on their heads.
They were arguing over heroism and misfortune.

The children weren't listening and were quick to leave the table as soon as they had permission, taking advantage of the general good will on holidays to engage in forbidden games, jumping on beds and swinging upside down.
But they held back everything.

Next to the fabulous times of which they would not organize the episodes for a long time, the Debacle, the Exodus, the Occupation, the Landing, the Victory they found dull that unnamed era in which they were growing up.
They regretted not being born, or barely born, when they had to set off in cohorts on the roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
They would hold a tenacious regret for this unexperienced time.
The memories of others passed onto them a secret nostalgia for that era they had just missed, and the hope to experience it one day.
The frenzy that followed the Liberation was fading.
So people could think of nothing but going out and the world was filled with desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first since the war caused a rush, bananas, National Lottery tickets, fireworks.

By whole neighborhoods, from the grandmother supported by her daughters to the infant in a baby carriage, people rushed to the fairgrounds, to the torchlight procession, to Bouglione circus where they narrowly escaped being trampled in the crowd.
They gathered in a praying and singing crowd on the road to welcome the statue of Our Lady of Boulogne and accompany her for miles the next day.
Secular or religious, any occasion was good for them to be outside together, as if they wanted to continue living collectively.
On Sunday evenings, the buses returned from the sea with tall young men in shorts who sang at the top of their lungs, climbed on the luggage racks.
The dogs roamed freely and mated in the middle of the street.
Family narrative and social narrative are one and the same.

The voices of the guests defined the spaces of youth: the countryside and farms where, from a forgotten past, men were appointed and girls became servants, the factory where they all met, fraternized and married, and the small businesses that had been attained by the most ambitious.

They depicted stories devoid of personal events other than births, marriages and mourning, without travels outside of the regiment to a distant garrison town lives filled with work, its hardship and wear, accompanied by the threat of alcohol.
The school had been a mythical background, a brief golden age with the teacher as its stern god wielding an iron ruler to rap knuckles.
From hand to hand, browned photos with backs tarnished by all the fingers that had held them at other meals were passed around, a mix of coffee and grease blended into an indefinable color.
In the stiff and serious newlyweds, with the wedding guests ranking in several rows along a wall, one could not recognize either their relatives or anyone else.
It wasn't oneself one saw in the half-naked, sex-indistinct baby on a cushion, but someone else, a creature belonging to a mute and inaccessible time.
